meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn't mind who gets the credit'?
meta.ogDescription: Reagan displayed it on his Oval Office desk, but he didn't coin it. The saying traces to an 1863 diary and Montague's 1922 Disenchantment.

answer.label: Not original to Reagan — an older anonymous saying he displayed
answer.sourceLine: Ronald Reagan kept this line on a plaque and quoted it in a 29 Feb 1988 speech — but he introduced it as “a little sign” on his desk, not his own words. Quote Investigator traces the idea to an 1863 diary record of the Jesuit Father Strickland, and the closest ancestor of this exact wording is Montague’s 1922 Disenchantment: “There is no limit to what a man can do so long as he does not care a straw who gets the credit for it.” The precise Reagan-era form has no identified author.

source.excerpt: On my desk in the Oval Office, I have a little sign that says: There is no limit to what a man can do or where he can go if he doesn’t mind who gets the credit.
trail: Quote Investigator traces this family of sayings to an 1863 diary entry recording the Jesuit Father Strickland, and finds the closest match to this wording in C.E. Montague’s 1922 Disenchantment: “There is no limit to what a man can do so long as he does not care a straw who gets the credit for it.”
In his 29 Feb 1988 remarks Reagan says: “On my desk in the Oval Office, I have a little sign that says…” — presenting the line as a saying, not his own coinage.
The Reagan Library confirms the plaque sat on his Oval Office desk but gives no author, and the Reagan Foundation files it under his quotes citing only that 1988 speech.
source.excerptNote: Reagan’s own framing in his 29 Feb 1988 remarks — he attributes the words to the sign, not to himself.

source.rightsNote: The idea is old and its early forms (Father Strickland, 1863; Montague’s 1922 Disenchantment) are public domain, but those use different wording. The exact Reagan-era phrasing — adding “or where he can go” — has no identified author or first-publication date, so no rights status can be responsibly asserted for this precise form.

author.name: Charles Edward Montague
author.heading: Charles Edward Montague
author.bio: Charles Edward Montague (1867–1928) was an English journalist, novelist and essayist who spent most of his career at the Manchester Guardian. His 1922 essay collection Disenchantment contains the closest documented ancestor of this line — though even Montague did not claim to have coined it, and Quote Investigator finds the underlying thought recorded decades earlier.

misattribution.heading: How Reagan got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most common Reagan attributions, but Reagan himself never claimed it — he read it off a sign.

items.why: Reagan kept the line on an Oval Office plaque and quoted it in his 29 Feb 1988 remarks, but introduced it as “a little sign that says…” — presenting it as an existing saying, not his own.

Quote Investigator gives primary credit for the family of sayings to the Jesuit Father Strickland, recorded in an 1863 diary: “A man may do an immense deal of good, if he does not care who gets the credit for it.”

The same thought is widely pinned to Truman (“It is amazing what you can accomplish if you do not care who gets the credit”) and to Benjamin Jowett; QI shows these are later branches of the older saying.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are an evolved anonymous aphorism — closest to Montague’s 1922 Disenchantment and rooted in an 1863 diary — that Reagan popularized by keeping it on his desk.

context.heading: Why the saying stuck to Reagan
lead: Reagan gave the line its modern fame not by writing it but by living with it: a small plaque on his Oval Office desk that he pointed to when praising people who worked without seeking recognition. When a president quotes a sign every so often, the sign’s words become his in the public memory.
The sentiment had already travelled for a century under many names before it reached that desk — which is exactly why the exact wording resists a single author.
context.pull: Reagan didn’t coin it. He read it off a sign — and the sign became the quote.
